vignette:
Leo is a 22-year-old undergraduate student majoring in international relations, sitting across from me for the fourth session. He is thin, with a neatly trimmed beard and dark circles under his eyes that no amount of coffee can mask. He speaks softly, often pausing to stare at the floor. He tells me he feels like he is living in two worlds at once, and neither one feels real.

Nine months ago, Leo was a different person. He had just finished his sophomore year when he joined a humanitarian aid organization as a volunteer in a conflict zone in the southern Shan State. He had wanted to make a difference, to see the suffering he read about in textbooks. For the first three weeks, his work was logistics-delivering food parcels to displaced families, helping set up temporary clinics. He remembers the dust, the heat, the constant hum of generators. He remembers the children who would wave at his convoy.

The trauma happened on a Tuesday afternoon. His team was returning from a distribution site when the truck ahead of them hit an improvised explosive device. The blast wave threw Leo against the side of his own vehicle. He remembers the ringing in his ears, the smell of burned rubber and something metallic. He scrambled out to help, but there was only smoke and twisted metal. He saw a colleague's shoe lying on the road, still laced. He tried to pull a man from the wreckage, but the man's arm came off in his hands. Leo vomited. Then he ran, not knowing where, until another aid worker found him hours later, shaking in a ditch.

He was evacuated two days later. The organization offered him counseling, but he declined. He told himself he was fine. He returned to campus in the fall, determined to pick up his old life. But the old life no longer fits.

Leo avoids the student union building because it reminds him of the crowded distribution points. He cannot walk past a construction site without his heart hammering-the sound of jackhammers is too close to the blast. He has stopped eating lunch in the dining hall because the clatter of trays and the sudden laughter of other students make him jump. He dropped his statistics class because the professor used a PowerPoint slide with a red circle, and Leo saw a sniper's reticle.

Nights are the worst. He sleeps in a corner of his dorm room, facing the door, with a chair wedged under the handle. He has nightmares three or four times a week: the same explosion, the same arm, but sometimes he is the one holding the detonator. He wakes up drenched in sweat, convinced he can smell diesel fuel. He has not told his roommate why he moved his mattress.

Academically, Leo is unraveling. He cannot concentrate on readings about peace treaties or economic development-they feel like lies. He finds himself staring at the ceiling during lectures, replaying the faces of the dead. His GPA has dropped from a 3.6 to a 2.1 this semester. His advisor has asked if he is struggling, but Leo says everything is fine. He does not want to be seen as weak.

He has stopped responding to texts from friends. He feels like they cannot possibly understand, and he does not have the energy to explain. When a classmate complains about a low grade, Leo feels a surge of rage so hot it scares him. He has started drinking alone in his room, just enough to quiet the images before sleep. He tells me he feels like he is already dead, just going through the motions. He feels guilty for being alive when his colleagues are not. He wonders if he should have tried harder, been braver, saved someone.

Last week, a leaflet from a campus volunteering fair appeared in his mailbox. He tore it into pieces without reading it. Then he picked up the pieces and threw them away, because he was afraid of what the sight of them might do. He came to see me because his academic dean required proof of a medical excuse for his absences. He does not think therapy will help. He says he just wants to sleep without waking up screaming.
